Syamantakamaṇi
------------------------------------------
Satrājita was a Yādava chieftain. Through severe austerities he had appeased सूर्य (the Sun-god). Pleased with him, सूर्य had given him a special gem called स्यमन्तकमणि which would yield 160 tolas (equivalent to 34 kgs.) of gold every day.
Satrājit had strung it into a necklace which could be worn whenever one liked.
Once Kṛṣna is said to have requested Satrājit to give it to him but Satrājit refused.
One day, Prasena, brother of Satrājit, wearing this necklace, went out hunting. A lion killed him and was taking the necklace away when जाम्बवान् (the king of bears, of the रामायण fame) encountered it, killed it and took the necklace to be given to Jāmbavatī his daughter. She tied it to the cradle of the baby in her होउसे.
When Satrājit heard that Prasena had been killed and that the necklace had been missing he suspected कृष्ण of stealing it. कृष्ण quickly searched for it, recovered it from जाम्बवान् and restored it to Satrājit.

Śyāmāśāstri
(A. D. 1763-1827)
------------------------------------------
Hindu मुसिच् has been predominantly spiritual in content and orientation. It has attained the status of a योग (‘nādayoga’).
During the period A. D. 1750-1850 three great musician-saints, who were also inspired composers, appeared in South India and enriched classical South Indian मुसिच्, also known as Carnatic मुसिच्. श्यामाशास्त्रि was the seniormost of them, the other two being त्यागराज (A. D. 1767-1847) and मुद्दुस्वामि दीक्षितर् (A. D. 1775-1835).
His parents were ब्राह्मणस्. They were originally from the Telugu country (now Andhra Pradesh). They were worshippers of goddess कामाक्षी of Kāñcī-puram (now in Tamil Nadu). From North India, they migrated to Tiruvārūr (in Tamil Nadu) due to the unsettled conditions created by frequent Muslim invasions. They had no issues.
By the grace of Lord Veṅkaṭesvara of तिरुपति to whom they were constantly praying, a son was born during A. D. 1763. An oracle had declared that this son would become very famous. He was named श्यामाशास्त्रि.
The boy was given very good एदुचतिओन् in Sanskrit and Telugu languages as also fundamentals of मुसिच्. He attained proficiency under a musician-monk and Ādiyappan, the most famous singer of those days.
As a result of devoted worship of the goddess कामाक्षी, he became highly inspired and started spontaneously composing songs of various types. He became an unparalleled expert in that field. Many an arrogant musician or detractor of his times was humbled by him in no time.
His compositions end with the aṅkita (assumed name) ‘Śyāmakṛṣṇa’.
He has 300 compositions to his credit. They are, generally speaking, difficult to master.
He had two sons. His second son Subbarāyaśāstri was an equally great musician.
